title: Question 5

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by rectification.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what goes into the bridge in Fig. 5.1 and what comes out across the resistor - how does the type of current change?
parts.proper_answer: Rectification is the conversion of alternating current (a.c.) to direct current (d.c.).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What the circuit does**
Think of $V_{IN}$ as a sine wave that keeps reversing direction. A useful d.c. supply must push charge one way only. Rectification is simply the name for that process of turning a reversing a.c. into a one-direction d.c.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: State the type of rectification produced by the circuit in Fig. 5.1.
hints: Hint 1: Count the diodes in Fig. 5.1 and recall what happens on both the positive and negative half-cycles of the input.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Half-wave versus full-wave**
With one or two diodes you can block one half of the input, giving half-wave. Here you have four diodes in a bridge. That steers current through the load in the same direction on both halves of the input, so both halves are used. That is full-wave rectification.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A sinusoidal alternating voltage $V_{IN}$ is applied across the input terminals $X$ and $Y$. The variation with time $t$ of $V_{IN}$ is given by the equation

$$V_{IN} = 6.0 \sin 25\pi t$$

where $V_{IN}$ is in volts and $t$ is in seconds.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 5.1, label the output terminals $P$ and $Q$ with the appropriate symbols to indicate the polarity of the output voltage $V_{OUT}$.
hints: Hint 1: Follow conventional current through the forward-biased diodes on one half-cycle and see which way it flows through the 1.2 kΩ resistor, from P to Q or Q to P.
parts.proper_answer: P is negative (-) and Q is positive (+), so conventional current flows from Q to P outside the resistor, i.e. downwards through $V_{OUT}$ is from Q (+) to P (-).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Trace the diode bridge**
A diode conducts only in the direction of its arrow (triangle to bar). On either half-cycle, one pair of opposite diodes is forward biased and the other pair is reverse biased. Whichever way X-Y polarity is, the bridge always routes current to enter the load at the same terminal.

Step 2: **Fix the polarity**
Tracing either half-cycle in Fig. 5.1 shows current flows upward through the resistor from Q toward P. So Q stays at higher potential. Label Q + and P -.

parts.label: (b)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: VOUT scale labelled 4 and 8 on the 2 cm tick marks
t scale labelled 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12 on the 2 cm tick marks

hints: Hint 1: Compare $V_{IN} = 6.0 \sin 25\pi t$ with the standard $V = V_0 \sin \omega t$ to pick out the peak value and the angular frequency.
Hint 2: Use $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi / T$ to find the input period, then think about why the rectified output repeats twice as often.
Hint 3: Decide what peak height and what time spacing the humps in Fig. 5.2 must have, then choose sensible numbers for the marked grid lines.
parts.proper_answer: Peak $V_{OUT} = 6.0\text{ V}$. Input period $T_{IN} = 2\pi/25\pi = 0.080\text{ s}$, so rectified period $T_{OUT} = 0.040\text{ s}$. Label $V_{OUT}$ axis e.g. 4 V and 8 V on successive 2 cm marks (peak at 6.0 V) and $t$ axis 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12 s on successive 2 cm marks.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the peak from the equation**
$$V_{IN} = 6.0 \sin 25\pi t$$ is of the form $$V = V_0 \sin \omega t$$ so $V_0 = 6.0\text{ V}$ and $\omega = 25\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}$. Ideal diodes drop no voltage, so the rectified peak is also $6.0\text{ V}$. That sets the height of every hump in Fig. 5.2.

Step 2: **Find the input period**
Angular frequency links to period by: $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$ $$T_{IN} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{25\pi} = 0.080\text{ s}$$ That is the time for one full sine wave at the input.

Step 3: **Halve the period for full-wave**
Full-wave turns the negative half-cycle positive, so you get two identical humps per input cycle. The output period is half the input period: $$T_{OUT} = \frac{0.080}{2} = 0.040\text{ s}$$ So zeros occur every $0.040\text{ s}$ and peaks are midway between zeros. Labelling the $t$-axis in steps of $0.020\text{ s}$ and the $V_{OUT}$-axis so the peak sits at $6.0\text{ V}$ completes Fig. 5.2.

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem: The output voltage in (b) is smoothed by adding a capacitor to the circuit in Fig. 5.1. The difference between the maximum and minimum values of the smoothed output voltage is 10% of the peak voltage.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 5.1, draw the circuit symbol for a capacitor showing the capacitor correctly connected into the circuit.

markscheme_points.text: correct symbol used for capacitor and capacitor connected in parallel with the 1.2

hints: Hint 1: Think where charge must be stored to keep current flowing through the load when the rectified voltage falls to zero - across which component should the capacitor sit?
parts.proper_answer: Connect a capacitor in parallel with the 1.2 kΩ load resistor, i.e. directly between P and Q.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Where smoothing happens**
Smoothing uses a large capacitor that charges to the peak and then discharges through the load when the supply dips. To do that it must see the same voltage as the load, so connect it across P and Q, in parallel with the $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor.

hints: Hint 1: Recall that the capacitor holds the voltage near the peak and only falls slowly while the rectified signal is below it.
Hint 2: Use the 10% ripple stated in (c) to judge how far the voltage should fall between peaks before it rises sharply to the next peak.
parts.proper_answer: Draw a small ripple on Fig. 5.2: voltage falls slowly with decreasing gradient from each 6.0 V peak to 5.4 V, then rises sharply to the next peak. Ripple $= 0.10 \times 6.0 = 0.60\text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Shape of smoothed output**
The capacitor charges quickly to the $6.0\text{ V}$ peak, then when the rectified wave falls, the capacitor discharges slowly through the $1.2\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor. So between peaks draw a gently falling line with negative decreasing gradient, not down to zero.

Step 2: **Size of the dip**
Maximum to minimum difference is 10% of peak: $$0.10 \times 6.0 = 0.60\text{ V}$$ So each dip goes from $6.0\text{ V}$ down to about $5.4\text{ V}$, then jumps steeply back up to the next $6.0\text{ V}$ peak.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the capacitance $C$ of the capacitor.

markscheme_points.text: V = 0.90 × 6.0 (= 5.4 V) or discharge time (for each cycle) = 0.034 s

hints: Hint 1: Work out the lowest voltage of the ripple from 10% of the 6.0 V peak.
Hint 2: Recall the equation for exponential discharge of a capacitor through a resistor and identify $V_0$, $V$, $R$ and $t$.
Hint 3: Rearrange $V = V_0 \exp(-t/RC)$ to solve for $C$, using discharge time about 0.034 s (approximately the 0.040 s ripple period minus charging time) and $R = 1.2\text{ k}\Omega$.
parts.proper_answer: Minimum $V = 5.4\text{ V}$, $R = 1.2 \times 10^3\ \Omega$, $t \approx 0.034\text{ s}$. Using $V = V_0 \exp(-t/RC)$ gives $C \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the discharge limits**
Peak $V_0 = 6.0\text{ V}$. Ripple is 10%, so drop $= 0.60\text{ V}$. Lowest voltage: $$V = 6.0 - 0.60 = 5.4\text{ V}$$ The capacitor discharges from $6.0\text{ V}$ to $5.4\text{ V}$ through $R = 1.2\times 10^3\ \Omega$ in time $t \approx 0.034\text{ s}$ per ripple cycle.

Step 2: **Apply exponential discharge**
Discharge follows: $$V = V_0 \exp\left(\frac{-t}{RC}\right)$$ Substitute: $$5.4 = 6.0 \exp\left[\frac{-0.034}{(1.2\times 10^3) C}\right]$$

Step 3: **Solve for C**
$$\frac{5.4}{6.0} = 0.90 = \exp\left[\frac{-0.034}{(1.2\times 10^3) C}\right]$$ Taking natural logs, $\ln 0.90 = -0.1053$, gives: $$C = \frac{0.034}{(1.2\times 10^3)\times 0.1053} \approx 2.7\times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$$ This large value gives a long time constant $RC$ for good smoothing.
